paragraphs.text: THE APOLOGETIC POEM OF COMMODIAN.
Who will be able truly to know the one God of the heavens,
unless he has drawn that person [?] away from abominable error?
I wandered, roaming in ignorance, captivated by empty hope,
while the frenzy of my early youth carried me off on the winds.
I was lighter than chaff; as though there were a hundred heads
on my shoulders, so headlong was I swept along wherever I went.
That was not enough: through these things I finally became a criminal,
almost a Marsian sorcerer, chanting spells over baleful herbs.
But thanks be to the Lord (my voice is not able to give thanks enough),
who at last shone upon me in my wretchedness and wavering!
And I set about searching the book of the law handed down to us
to learn what was in it; at once a lamp shone for me.
Then indeed I recognized the one God, most high in the heights,
and therefore I urge people like me to turn back from error.
Who is a better physician than one who has suffered the burning of a wound?
Many indeed, dull and ignorant, asleep in heart,
set themselves to learn nothing; like wild beasts
they look for what they may seize, or on whose blood they may live.
As long as they are glad to live like fattened pigs,
they heap up dishes like a burial mound, while they applaud their riches.
[?] They will be changed [?] into poor clothing, with disdain [?].
Surely what they eat more readily would be enough for them.
If a man is fat with wealth, let it be his; if he is worthy of Caesar,
why does he, frail as he is, put his own things first and have regard for no one?
Rather, let such a man share his goodness with all,
a man to whom the Most High has granted riches and lofty honours.
For I do not condemn riches given by the Most High,
but he will deserve blame who is puffed up by them above others.
So now I urge all of you, high and lowly alike,
to read constantly either these things or the rest of the law.
Look, for the life entrusted to us is short;
learn, you who are wise, why we who are born must die!
Why do we die dull-witted? What has it profited us to have seen the light?
If you inquire into nothing, that is to live like the beasts.
Surely God most high set man over the fields,
not a wild beast or cattle. Why should we make ourselves like them?
The Almighty willed that man should offer him praise;
therefore he himself taught us the divine things to come.
And so that we might believe them, he did not merely sound forth in words,
but also showed mighty works when Pharaoh was deceived.
Nor did he do only this: in the times of Noah too
he showed what he could do, since no one was seeking God.
After that he began little by little to be present more gently,
once the flood had come, so that the earth could be filled again.
Already nearly half of six thousand years was passing,
and no one knew the Lord, and people lived at random.
But God, when he saw that the hearts of men were all too closed,
speaks to Abraham, of whom Moses himself tells.
He gave the law to the people once Pharaoh had been killed,
and through Moses the Lord himself declared beforehand who he was.
Nor does he reveal himself content with a single prophetic voice,
but he called on many witnesses, who cry out about him.
This one, then, when you read the proclamations of many prophets,
you will find to have taken on flesh for us.
That is why people now go astray, [denying] that the Most High ordained such things,
and they sneer, as it were, not knowing that they are laughed at by him!
Meanwhile I add how I have read through the prophets,
and I teach the untaught where the hope of life should be placed.
What God did first, and how he made each thing,
Moses has already taught; but we teach about Christ.
I am not a prophet, nor a teacher commanded to be one,
but I lay out the predictions of the prophets for those who drift with the south winds.
So you who are like me, whom the wind carries headlong away,
seek now the harbour, where there are no dangers.
The skilled farmer recognizes the coming storms from far off
and, before they arrive, takes refuge in a cave.
Be wise: see beforehand what threatens,
and before disasters come, look to your salvation.
Idleness belongs to boys, certainly not to grown men:
if it befits the untrained, it does not suit those of mature age.
Any man who has not been tempered will, when he is old,
be like a ham that has hardly been salted: he will rot.
Nothing subdues a rock except fire alone, which feeds on it:
so stony men soften too late, in Gehenna.
We cry out in vain, our words carried back to us by deaf storms,
and we offer light to the blind, giving it to no purpose.
A soldier stands to hear the orders: one listens, another shrugs them off
and does not take the warnings to heart, but wanders, lost.
Who then is at fault (you be the judges of this!):
the one who warns, or the one who will not obey what is said?
I trust he is not guilty who obeys Caesar's word,
but the proud man who opposes it loses his life.
Meanwhile, as is my part, I who once went astray show
the right road to you who still wander aimlessly.
Yet you must choose, as your own judgment pleases,
which you want: poison, or the sweet cups of life!
Good and evil have been created in this nature of things,
so that after death man may be tested as to who is worthy of God.
Set out now, whoever you are, to know the things that last for ever:
learn who God is, and in whose name he is present!
God is almighty, one, created from himself,
whom you will find below to be both great and lowly.
He was set in the Word, known to himself alone,
he who is called Father and Son and Holy Spirit.
But from the time he decided to compose the world with its constellations,
he set between a fire that the angels themselves must fear.
These he appointed, made of lesser power,
to rule the heavens and the earth and what lies beneath the earth.
So not even the messengers themselves can discern
what he is like or how great, except that they follow his commands.
His glory is hidden from us and from the angels themselves,
for what God's majesty is, it alone knows.
It shines out, immeasurable, above the heavens and without end;
it is all golden, for it is like a fiery power.
There is God's vessel, but without any known form;
those are the secrets of the heavens, known to God alone.
This is the unique glory of God, above all the angels;
this is the God of eternal light, this the Spirit of eternity.
What he is in his original state no one sees;
he is transfigured as he wishes to show himself.
He makes himself visible to angels in a form like theirs,
and to man he becomes man; otherwise God is known through the Word.
Therefore the form of so great a God cannot be discerned;
whatever he is, he is one, alone in immeasurable light;
where a face, eyes, a mouth or limbs are ascribed to him,
it is in the sense that he holds the circle of the world enclosed in his fist.
And yet when he wished it to be known who he was,
from so great a divinity he made himself seen in a form that could be contained.
To some he appeared in fire, speaking with a voice;
he whom no region could contain was taken up into flesh.
This almighty God, Lord of his creation,
though invisible, makes himself seen by some.
Now he takes a form, now he spreads himself out into the air,
and it is not lawful to seek his beginning or his end.
He is God always, without beginning and without end,
who, before he made the heaven, moved through eternity;
whatever the heaven holds he looks upon everywhere from heaven,
and he penetrates all things with his eyes, and hears with his ears.
It pleased him, then, to set up the fleshly order of the world,
so that his everlasting majesty alone might be exalted.
For to tell what was before is now a hard matter;
though it may have been described, let us not trouble ourselves with those things.
When we cannot grasp in full even these things we see,
who will be able to know what lies beyond the end of the Ocean?
We see the heaven too, but what goes on within it
no one is given to know until the end of the age comes.
Let it be enough for us to know the promises about the future;
let us strive eagerly toward them, devoted with our whole mind.
Just as the bird, the phoenix, plans to be reborn from death,
it gives us an example that one can rise after death;
this, above all, almighty God urges us to believe:
that a time will come when the dead live again;
though a man be dust now, though his bones lie bare,
one day the man who had died will be made whole,
and then there will be grace greater than that of this age;
then there will be no pain or tears in our body,
the flesh will not take a sword's wound, no sore will rise.
God will establish this, so that his glory may be greater.
He had made the first man to be eternal,
but that man fell into death by neglecting the commands.
For this reason God arranged so many dispensations in history,
to wipe away all the devices of the devil.
God had given this angel as ruler on earth;
but in envying man he himself perished first.
Meanwhile God distinguishes the righteous by their deeds,
and keeps the wicked Cain for Gehenna.
The whole human race began to live in crime,
with no regard for who their creator was.
Because God on high bore this with indignation,
he resolves to destroy nearly all that he had created.
It is said and read that Noah was delivered from the water;
the rest perished in the flood from heaven.
From then on, as in the beginning, the earth is gradually filled again.
The former crime ceased, but another disaster took hold.
Fools set about building a tower up to the stars,
so that through it, as it were, they could climb into heaven.
When God saw this being done by people of one speech,
he came down and made them speak different tongues.
From there he scattered them apart over the islands of the earth,
so that they became nations speaking varied languages.
Then the untaught race lived a life of savagery;
no one knew God, no one reasoned about life.
For that reckless one had crept in upon the untaught
through the waters of the soul, and corrupted their harsh minds,
and by guile persuaded them to love unspeakable unions,
to live by plunder, rejoicing in bloodshed.
This glory fools pursue for a short time;
then no pardon frees them, though they say they were led astray.
If the adulterer tempts you, the fault is yours for following such a one;
it is not he who condemns you, but you who condemn yourself of your own will.
The untaught went astray through the deceit of the ancient enemy,
forgetting the Lord and following evil works.
So that the robber's great rampage might not last long,
God at last took pity, and the time allotted to it was cut off.
It pleased him to speak with one man out of many,
to make a people beloved to him by its crossing over to him.
From that man the profane began to know the one God
and to become a people according to God's decrees.
For Rebecca had brought forth from herself two distinct peoples:
this one came first, so that the other might succeed it.
Israel grew up first in Egypt, like a nursling;
from there God brought them out under the leadership of Moses,
through whom he gave them the law on Mount Sinai,
so that our posterity might know the one Lord.
Then he commanded prophets from among them to declare
that God, become man, would be held cheap by them.
The Lord had led them into the promised land,
so that they might live there under the law until he himself should come.
The nation, ungrateful for good things, refused to bear the yoke of the commandments,
but rather fell back into its old wickedness and flourished in it;
nor did it ever stop: today too it is held to be the same;
passing God by, it prefers the luxuries of the world.
This the Lord especially urges his beloved to shun;
he warns them beforehand to be wholly cut off from the world.
If he has called us sons, let us dwell in his holy things;
why do we go outside, following the adulterer's pomp?
The ancient seducer deceives everyone through such things:
he sends in luxuries, through which to destroy the sons of the Most High;
he sends in games, urging people to go to bloody spectacles
or to utterly obscene ones, so that the chaste may learn unchastity.
If a man was chaste, he becomes unchaste as a result,
and the evil pleasures that then tempt him please him and smile upon him.
In these luxuries the first people lived,
and always strayed monstrously from the law of God.
To cleanse them God often sent his own servants,
to bring them, corrupted as they were, back again to the Most High.
They never would receive the divine words,
but always raged senselessly according to their own will.
They wickedly slaughtered the righteous who rebuked them,
since they would not accept the bridle of heavenly discipline.
They saw Isaiah in two, in their arrogance they stone Jeremiah,
they behead John, they slaughter Zechariah at the altar.
And then he himself came, the one whom they had foretold,
and suffers, as he willed, in our likeness.
In his death all prophecy was fulfilled;
Daniel had said that he would be the last of the prophets.
He was the one for whose sake the prophets sang as with a trumpet
that he would come to his own, and his own would deny him.
Ever heedless, stiff-necked, kicking back,
in rejecting his form they lose the sacraments of the law.
They were not broken by the righteousness of the humble one born in the flesh,
nor by such great goodness, nor by his care for the sick through his word.
O holy religion, O majesty so worthy of reverence,
whose medicine did such good on earth!
He cut no one with a knife, he healed no one with a plaster,
but healed at once by his word, without torment.
Seeing such things, the Jews were troubled in mind,
driven rather by envy into the zeal of spite,
paying no regard to the words of the prophets now buried,
that such a man would come as would scatter them.
Until the Lord should come, the prophets sang;
from the time he came, prophecy fell silent for the Jews.
After him they went into exile with hardened hearts,
and even now they do not discern why they have suffered such things.
It had been foretold to them by the prophet Isaiah,
and likewise by Daniel, that they would lose their land;
yet not before the leader of the city should hang on the wood
within it; then it would become desolate.
How suddenly glory shone upon a nation,
so that a people came to be that before was no people!
Was not Esau, beloved of his father, dumbfounded
that his younger brother should carry off the birthright?
Just so the synagogue could not recognize the time
when, and under what leader, it would fall from its privilege;
as it was written, that the birds know their seasons,
but this people has not understood that I was present.
The time came for the ruler of heaven himself to come:
according to the Scriptures, he was not esteemed by them.
The Lord had foreknown this, as one who knows all things;
therefore he foretold these things through the mouths of the prophets.
A nation exceedingly stiff-necked and always rebellious,
while claiming primacy for itself, had its case cut off.
In their place in the race he set the Gentiles first;
he had said this beforehand: The Gentiles will hope in him.
For he himself is the stone laid in the foundations of Zion,
so that whoever believed in him would have eternal life.
Daniel indicates that this Holy of Holies would be anointed,
and that after him the royal anointing would be destroyed.
David said that he would be fastened with nails, in silence:
"They pierced my hands and my feet," he says.
Solomon too prophesies so openly about him,
that the Jews would say, "Let us kill the righteous man!"
Jeremiah likewise shows the cross in a figure,
when they say, "Come, let us put wood into his bread!"
And their own leader, Moses, proclaims to them:
"Before your eyes your life will hang, put to death."
Here the Father came in the Son, one God everywhere:
nor would he be called Father had he not become the Son.
For he did not leave heaven in order to appear on earth,
but, as he had arranged, the majesty was seen on earth;
by his own power he caused himself to be born in the flesh
[?] it is permitted to make a single fringe [?].
Now God was flesh, and in that flesh God's power was at work.
What of the fact that the prophets sing that the invisible would be seen,
so that such great brightness would become man too, for our sake?
Nor would our people have sprung forth into the new law
had the Almighty not ordained it beforehand concerning us.
He was the Almighty, in whose name the nations
would believe wholly, as the prophet Isaiah said:
"A man will rise in Israel from the root of Jesse;
in him the nations will hope, and by his sign they are protected."
And another said that he would be a witness throughout the world,
that he himself would be revealed as prince to the nations.
In the Psalms it is sung: "The Lord has reigned from the tree;
let the earth exult, let the many islands rejoice."
So too the true blessing of the patriarch Jacob
was made plain among the Gentiles: "He will be the hope of the nations," he says.
Under heaven there is no other name set above all but the name of Christ,
in whose name the nations everywhere have believed.
We are not urged to believe for the sake of a limited time,
but for the time to come, when we shall live in eternity.
This is the hope we must cherish: to enjoy what is everlasting,
not these things which, frail as they are, quickly change our joys.
Though riches lie before your eyes to be lavishly enjoyed,
you are shut out from them when fleeting death takes their place;
or if you live on and on, you shudder at living itself;
or if your health is bad, what good is life to you?
All that we live through in this age is torment;
so it is in the future that we must seek our hope:
to this God urges us, to this the law, to this the passion of Christ,
that we believe we shall rise again in the new age.
Thus God's law cries out: when the Most High should become lowly,
hell would give way, so that Adam might be raised from death.
The Lord, pitying the creature he had formed, went down into the tomb,
and so by hidden means emptied death of its strength.
The Lord crept up on the ancient robber in disguise
and was willing to suffer, the better to overthrow him.
That one, bold indeed and always savage as an enemy,
while hoping to rage against a man, is conquered by the Most High.
By the very means through which the malicious one had once laid man low in death,
by that same means he was defeated; and from this life comes to us.
Adam, having tasted the fruit, was sentenced to die, and died;
and through his sin all of us likewise die in the same way.
But again the Lord said: "If he takes from the tree of life,
let him live for ever in honour."
Death was in a tree, and in a tree life lay hidden,
the tree on which God the Lord hung, the discoverer of our life.
The Lord had foretold that this was the tree of life,
so that whoever believes in him is as though he took from it.
And he takes and sweetly tastes the commands of God most high,
and departs from death, since he rises the stronger.
Whoever believes in Christ tastes of the tree of life
on which the Lord was hanged, as Moses foretold.
Isaiah declares this very one to be lowly
and greatly cast down, as if in the form of a slave:
"And we saw him, and he had no splendid appearance,
a man laid low in affliction, who knew how to bear all things.
He grieves for us and carries our sins,
and for our wrongdoing God handed him over."
When he was tormented, he was silent like a lamb at the altar.
He was now no mere man, but God made flesh for us;
by which it plainly appears that this name of God arose
which is now held to be a glorious name among the nations.
This the prophet Malachi sings, who is himself also a messenger,
when he rejects the sacrifices of the Jews, saying:
"Your sacrifice will not be acceptable to me,
but in every place the nations make offerings to my name,
among whom my name is magnified exceedingly,
and they offer to my name in purity, without blood."
For he himself was lowly, his great name hidden,
who cries out about himself through the mouths of the prophets:
"I am not stubborn," he says, "nor do I resist the one who harms me;
I gave my back to the whips to be beaten,
and offered my cheeks to be struck by wicked hands,
and I did not turn my face away from their spitting."
To many it has seemed folly that God suffered such things,
that the creator of the world should be proclaimed as crucified.
So it pleased him, taking no one's counsel
(nor could anyone else do it), to come in this way for us.
The enemy, in his envy, invented death,
and the Lord, by suffering, drank it up, rising again from hell.
That is why he did not wish to reveal what he was,
but said that he was the Son sent by the Father.
Thus he himself had appointed that the prophets should speak of him,
that God on earth would be the Son of the Most High.
This he himself also proclaimed aloud when he was lowly in the flesh,
and he calls the Father to witness, to confirm the words of the prophets.
We read that such a man would rise from Israel:
"And he is a man," it says, "and who among them has known him?"
Jeremiah says: "This is our God; none is equal to him;
after this he was seen on earth, living among men."
And Isaiah: "You are God, and we did not know it;
and God is in you, and besides you there is no other."
And who would come when the law of the prophets was setting?
"Sing to the Lord; God is the name of him who comes!"
And the forty-fourth psalm says of him:
"I shall be exalted among the nations with a great name."
And elsewhere we read: "Today I have begotten you, my son;
ask, and I will give it to you, and you will have the nations as your inheritance."
Surely it is now plain who God is and who is in him,
and in whose name we Gentiles everywhere were to believe:
this was said to "my Christ, whose right hand I hold":
"Let the nations hear, and let him rule over the nations."
What need is there of more, when the matter is so plainly proved,
when the people that was foretold [?] now rejoices in him?
But those wretches who embroider empty tales
and slander him as a magician [?] would have mocked [?] the beaks of those who sing [?].
What shall I call them? Before they were scattered,
they were men whom neither exile nor slavery itself could break.
If he was a magician, why then did the prophets sing
that he would come from heaven to be himself the hope of the nations?
If the prophets falsely declared of them that they would lose their land,
which has in fact happened to them, then what they said of him will also be false.
But because they are always despised, since they were bloodthirsty,
they rebel against their Lord by calling him a magician.
Nor will they hear what the prophets said against them:
that they would understand nothing at all, right up to the very end.
God himself described them: "With closed hearts
let them neither see with their eyes nor understand with their hardened hearts;
for the heart of this wicked people has grown fat,
so that they recognize nothing until they are healed by my word."
It was foretold that God would be born in the flesh for us,
so that their torment might deservedly be the greater:
"Behold, God himself will give you a sign from on high:
a virgin will conceive, and the earth will bring forth the heavenly one;
and he shall be called Emmanuel," he had told them,
which in the Latin tongue means "God with us."
Hear that he would be fed on honey and butter,
and would capture Samaria before he could speak a word.
But this is a hidden history, which the learned ponder over:
that a nursing infant should take spoils without a battle.
His passion was foretold in this way beforehand:
that God would become capable of suffering, his blood poured out.
Isaiah says: "Like a sheep led to the altar,
he did not cry out with his voice"; he bore everything patiently.
He is fastened with nails, as David had foretold long ago;
and they gave him vinegar to drink, according to the Scriptures.
"And for my clothing," he said, "they cast lots,"
which was done, and we read that it was all carried out in him.
There was also darkness for three hours from the sixth hour,
and the day hurried on, bringing out the stars of night.
This had been foretold through the prophet Amos:
that the day would suddenly hide itself during the holy feast.
O evil brood, [?] with deceitful faces!
"I have begotten children," said God, "who would deny me."
And he said, "Hear the sound of the trumpet." "We will not," they say.
So says Ezekiel: "Then the nations will hear from afar."
I wish to touch on the book of Deuteronomy with a single text:
"You nations will be the head; but the unbelieving will be the tail."
If these rebels indeed reject everything said above,
do you know what they can set against it, when the matter is stated so plainly?
See now, then, you who until now have been floundering in doubt,
that in the Lord's Scripture the Gentiles came first.
Now therefore it is right to believe in the one whom the books point to,
not in empty idols, which are worshipped in vain for the sake of life,
nor to join these pleasure-lovers who live without restraint,
who love luxuries more than the commands of the Most High.
Those who refuse to believe are guilty of more than one fault,
for they even slander him: "We threw him into a pit."
That is why the Lord in his indignation rebukes [?] them:
"Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations," he says.
If he was thrown into a pit, why then is it proclaimed that he rose again?
"From the underworld, O Lord, you have brought up [?] my soul";
"I slept," he says, "and took my rest secure;"
By the Lord's help I rose again, having suffered no harm.
And again he says: You will not abandon me in hell,
Nor will you let your holy one see destruction either.
Here he cries aloud: Sons of the prophet, I go higher,
To tell how the Lord, the Most High, suffered in misery.
In the book of Psalms, too, the Lord's death is proclaimed,
And it is not, as they suppose, David speaking of himself.
Or if they think so, does everything he said fit him?
David was not scourged, nor lifted up on a cross.
What? Do the Jews prophesy after the fashion of Saturn?
Do they band together in fables, when the matter already turns against them?
Did they not slap him like a criminal when he was lifted on the cross?
They invent such things for the unknowing, the untaught, the ignorant.
“Who is that God, whom we fastened to a cross?” they say,
Unwilling to look at the Scriptures, blind in heart.
See, another prophet sings it, repeating it once more,
And through his voice such an edict is proclaimed:
Now I will arise, says the Lord, now I will be glorified,
Now I will be exalted, I whom you saw lowly before;
Now you understand, now your confusion will come:
You think vain thoughts, and therefore fire will hold you.
So says Isaiah. Then the Majesty itself, in the same way,
When it was in the flesh, declared who it was:
No one, however he tries, will be able to take away my life,
But I lay it down freely of myself, by my own decree.
I myself have the power to lay it down,
And I have the power to take it up again.
More openly still the death of the righteous one is proclaimed,
So that it may be all the plainer that the Jews are hardened:
See, the righteous one perishes, and no one understands;
But the burial of this beloved one will be in peace.
Why do they slander him, saying he was thrown down into a pit,
When we read that he was given burial?
Shameful, cruel, blind, proud,
They applaud, who ought rather to mourn over the deed!
For Solomon, inspired, prophesies of him
And goes further, to portray the righteous one more fully:
Let us lie in wait for the righteous man, since he seems burdensome to us,
Who stands firmly against us, opposed to our works;
He reproaches us that we keep nothing at all of our law,
And he even affirms that he is the son of the Most High.
In every way he condemns us and reckons us triflers;
He keeps himself apart from us and goes another way;
He calls us unclean and brings in new and different ways of righteousness,
And he rejoices that the Lord of heaven is his father.
So let us prove whether his words are true;
Let us test this God, watching what becomes of him;
Let us question him, quiet as he is, with every torment;
Let us condemn him to a most shameful death,” they said.
When they had done these things, they wagged their heads and jeered:
Let the Father save him, or let him come down from there!
So that Solomon might openly show them to be blind,
He speaks as if he were telling it now, and blames them for having done such things:
While they thought these things, they were led into unspeakable error;
Their malice blinded them, so that they raged.
See, since they are blind themselves and call others blind,
Solomon said of them: They did not know the secrets of God.
Whatever all the earlier witnesses said
Came to pass in Christ. Or would they say it was in someone else?
If they wish to do just that, deceiving with their mouths,
Let them mock themselves; let them see it fulfilled in him.
Who was this righteous one of whom the prophets sang,
Since no one on earth is righteous, unless he had come from heaven?
For David the prince sinned by loving a young woman,
And Solomon sinned too; yet they repented.
Since these, such famous and distinguished kings of theirs,
Were not righteous, but themselves sang of the righteous one,
Nor did Isaiah the prophet say such things of himself,
He who was sawn in two by King Manasseh.
One was stoned, another slaughtered at the altar,
Another Herod ordered beheaded in prison.
All these prophets were cut off by other kinds of death,
Whereas the Lord hung on the tree, according to the word of Moses:
“Not as a man is God hanged,” he intimated beforehand;
“Nor does he suffer threats as a son of man,” he says.
So when the Lord himself had come, following these words,
He said: I must be rejected, according to the word of Moses.
But I do not gather the whole, only the highest peaks,
So that the ignorant may more easily learn the truth.
But these wicked men, who seek to live by guile,
Once stained with blood, persist in inventing empty tales.
With their words they befool the foolish into growing still more senseless,
Because he was crucified, when it was necessary that he be so.
For he arranged it thus because of the fall of the first man;
Not for him only, but for us too he came from heaven.
He established a new people, made firm in his name;
Christ fulfilled all things in accordance with the prophecies.
See, I make new things, Isaiah proclaims of him,
And let no one consider the former things, nor follow the old.
These are the new things that have come forth today under our law:
That we Gentiles have believed in Christ, according to the word of Moses.
He had foretold that there would be two peoples,
And he said, indeed, that the younger people would excel.
But these men, full of wickedness, now in desperate fury
Say: The law was given to us; where did you come from?
If they oppose us, they think they can resist the Most High as well,
Who willed to be good to us [?]
Nor do these stiff-necked men, their bristles raised, consider
That they have always tortured the innocent, corrupting the law.
So, cruel as they were, they did to God what they were used to doing,
And still they dare to call themselves sons of the Most High.
How he rose again I have already set down above;
I spoke not in my own words, but in the sayings of the prophets.
He had foretold everything about himself to his disciples:
How he would suffer at the hands of the people, while Peter denied him;
And that he would rise from the tomb on the third day,
He had said this too, and he fulfilled all that he had said.
And when he had risen, he came himself to the apostles
And stood in their midst. Peace be with you, he said.
Of the disciples gathered in prayer, one was not present;
When they told him, he would not believe, and added:
Unless I first put my finger where the nails were,
Or where he was pierced by the lance, I will not believe.
Then on the Lord's day he came back to them again
And stood in their midst. Peace be with you, he said.
And at once he went up to the unbelieving Thomas:
Come closer and touch my body, as it was before.
I am not a shade, such as the dead are thought to be:
A shade leaves no footprint; look at the wound.
He stretched out his palms; and Thomas began to touch them,
And into his side, where the lance had been driven, he put his hand,
And then threw himself down in prayer:
You are truly my God and my Lord! And he answered him:
Because you have seen this, you have believed; but blessed are those
Who come after, who believe having only heard the name.
For forty days in succession he stayed with them,
And taught them many things that would come upon the world.
After his ascension they worked many miracles;
With a word they healed the sick in the name of Christ.
If he were such as these faithless men say,
Mighty works would not have been done through him at the word of his witnesses.
He ascended into heaven, as Scripture had also sung:
Receive the King, you princes, in the heights of heaven!
What more need is there to recite everything from the law?
These things are enough for beginners, to be kept with a good heart.
But if they themselves will not come to know God by reading these things,
Let them blame themselves when they come where they do not wish to go.
Virgil is read, and Cicero or Terence likewise;
They do nothing but sharpen the wits; about life they are silent.
What good is it to chase vainly after worldly things on earth,
And to learn of the vices of kings and of their wars?
Or to get to know the mad forum, skilled in law,
Where the laws totter unless perhaps they are steered by a bribe?
A man may be an advocate, he may be an orator divine,
Yet he will gain nothing at death, if while living he denied Christ.
Rather, let him first ask where his life is laid up!
Then he would be wise, even if in other respects he is reviled.
They read the laws and learn marvelous forms of pleading,
But by their pleading they get the better of the poor wretches they speak for.
Unhappy is the man who falls into their mouths;
They carry off the praise, and he a victory at his own loss.
The wretch stands mute in the middle, grieving more within;
They thunder with their mouths, and he pays in silence, with his coins.
Meanwhile the ornate voice keeps up its daily din,
And often a bad cause is made the better by giving a little more.
Hence the wise man seeks his fee, hence he rejoices to win;
Though he act crookedly, so long as he only wins, he is sick at heart.
While he strives for gain, he does nothing for his own cause;
He takes up another's hope and puts his own behind him.
Many are carried off by success into the forest of this world;
While they rejoice in brief things, they remain apart from the grace of Christ;
While their eyes covet many things, while they seek to increase,
God is nothing to them, only the life of this world.
They toil for the belly; for it there is a daily contest,
And they scorn the true contest for eternal salvation.
Whoever keeps watch, so to speak, over his purse is praised as shrewd;
But whoever follows God is judged a buffoon by them.
O happy beyond measure is he who shuns worldly things!
Let him be a fool to others, so long as he is wise to God most high.
This is our whole hope: to believe in God, who hung on the tree;
It is a shameful thing, granted, but profitable for the life to come.
For that first people was deceived by this,
That he spoke of a son, when he himself is the God of old.
He went before them in the pillar of cloud and fire,
When he freed them from Egypt, every one of them.
He commanded a cruel crime concerning an only son,
To test Abraham, to whom from heaven an angel
Said: Spare him! And he is God, and he likewise made himself man,
And whatever he wills he will do, so that dumb things speak.
He made Balaam's ass speak to him as he sat on it,
And a dog, to tell Simon: You are summoned by Peter!
So that many might tell of him, while Paul was preaching
He made a lion speak to the people with a divine voice.
Then, a thing our nature does not allow,
He made an infant five months old speak out to the crowd.
He was to come mingled with our blood,
So that he would seem a man, while God lay hidden in the flesh.
Neither an elder nor an angel will come, said Isaiah,
But the Lord himself will come to show himself to us.
The sea feared him, the winds feared him, Tartarus itself feared him;
All creation recognized the hidden Lord.
Only the wicked people raised its [?] against him:
“Far be it that the Lord should have come in such a form!”
He walked upon the waves of the sea as on land
And commanded the winds, to make the sea calm.
He broke the law of Tartarus with a word spoken in person
And raised Lazarus from the tomb on the fourth day, already stinking.
For to the one who was being carried out, when he met him, he said:
Arise, young man! And he rose from the bier.
The daughter of the ruler of the synagogue, at her father's plea,
Already lifeless, he raised up while they mourned her.
He made the mute speak and, above all, the deaf hear,
And one blind from birth see the light of day.
After thirty-eight years he ordered a paralytic to rise,
And they marveled at him carrying his pallet on his neck.
When his garment was touched, a woman was healed of her flow of blood.
He broke five loaves for five thousand men
And again fed four thousand from seven.
So that the Lord might show more fully that he was present,
He changed water so that it became the finest wine.
He had been invited to a wedding together with his mother;
When he was asked to help because the wine had run out,
He then ordered the jars to be quickly filled with water,
Which he tasted first, and then ordered it to be served.
Not even so could they recognize the Lord by his deeds,
But they raged to put him to death as a wicked man.
This he allowed, since he had decreed to suffer so;
Yet if they believe, then at last they will have pardon.
This is the firstborn foretold beforehand by the prophets,
To be called on earth the offspring of the Most High.
Happy are those among men who put their hope in him,
But the foolish shun him as something accursed.
Eternity is prepared for whoever believes in Christ,
So that man, living on after death, may be God's companion.
The Law and the Prophets teach who are worthy of God's heavens
And to whom the hidden golden ages are revealed.
By so many prophets the Son of God is proclaimed,
And those first called sons of God shut their eyes;
Having done the crime, they did not call it to mind when they read,
But persist in saying: We are the chosen!
Still they befool the profane into going to baths,
Claiming that they make them clean to please the God most high.
Water washes off dirt, not the inner wickedness of the heart,
Nor could sacred rites, however carefully performed, wash the sacrilegious.
The Lord did not command that sacred things be given to the wicked;
And he said again that they must be kept clean of idols:
Let no one make himself an image of a demon, he says;
For he also told them: Do not serve idols.
If God commanded that idols be strictly avoided,
Why do they deceive the Gentiles into thinking they are made pure by washings?
Rather, when they receive such people, they ought to teach them
To serve no others, and to seek only to please the Most High.
While they seek to cover over their crime of Christ's death,
They throw open their doors to all, so that anyone may come in to them.
Hence those perish who think that by water they can become pure
And belong to God, though before they were in league with a robber.
Now that ignorant man worships anything at all in vain, now seeks holy things;
He does not know where to run first,
And he serves idols, and then again seeks the thirtieth day;
Now he follows unleavened bread, who earlier had kept a ritual fast.
It did not please God that men should be partners with demons,
He who established the law so that there might be a passing over from them.
Two ways are set before you: choose which you will,
For you cannot split yourself so as to walk both;
But you must seek out the right one of the two;
Be the more careful, lest you fall into the jaws of robbers.
Seek the one God, who seeks no sacrificial victims,
So that, washed clean, you may rise again when the age is renewed.
Why do you heed the wicked and judge the holy to be unjust,
When they show you not a single word from the law?
They tell of the power of God that he displayed among them;
But of their own wicked deeds they will not speak,
Murderers always, always with bloodstained hands,
Whom the Lord could never tame by warning.
It was enough for them to have done so much in their senselessness
And to say: So it was written; now it is right to believe.
But the Lord himself darkened their understanding;
He hardened them among themselves, as he had hardened Pharaoh;
Nor did he say he would hear their prayers,
And in anger he cast them out of their land.
Since he had indeed called them sons before,
He required that his sons live with a good heart;
For a father rejoices when his son is good to him;
But if he is bad, he curses the son with hatred.
No one endures having a son who sets himself against him;
All love is shut out from a cruel son,
Nor does the father make him sole heir of his goods,
Rather, if he can use them up first, he rejoices over him.
An impious and savage offspring, a tyrant over his property,
The father, provoked by him, cannot even bear to meet.
What do these men presume, adopted as they are, when they say:
Of all peoples we are the dearest to the Most High?
One who is ever his father's murderer and proud against him,
Can he be dear, or rightly be called heir?
If fathers in the flesh detest such children,
How much more the Lord, who has sons in plenty to choose from!
It is to gentle, humble children, full of obedience,
That the goods are divided, not to the impious or to tyrants.
The Jews had clearly been adopted as sons,
But in the testament they obtained the name of the impious.
Let them blame themselves: once they had committed the crime, stained with blood,
How could they possibly share in the inheritance?
Why do they gnash their teeth at us, why envy us as heirs?
Had they done good, they too would have shared in the legacy.
Even today they are not silent, and they refuse to believe in Christ,
Who had been foretold to them in the law as their Savior;
Of whom you have already heard how the prophets sang:
That the Lord would come to earth, and the nations would worship him.
Surely they urge us to recognize this very one as the Most High,
Who renews man and forgives former sins.
For he himself also threatens the worshipers of gods:
Whoever sacrifices to idols will perish in the second death.
So whoever follows gods fashioned of gold,
Of silver or stone, of wood, or cast in bronze,
Will be cast, unhappy man, into the fire with them, his body restored,
And there he does not die outright, but, wicked as he is, pays in torments.
There are men like cattle in this life,
Who wander about, unwilling to take the bridle of God most high;
Yet they themselves cannot bear such things from their slaves,
And they often savagely shed their slaves' blood.
They go on to say: “There is nothing after our death;
While we live, this is all there is”; and they wallow like swine;
“Let no luxury pass us by in our lifetime;
While there is time for life, let us enjoy everything in the world.”
Undisciplined, they spurn the mercy of God,
Chasing after merrymaking, as if this life were the only one.
So they turn away from God, who promises everlasting life:
They fight against the good, when it is the wicked that must be fought.
We all plainly went astray, won over by the world,
But by the grace of the Lord we are called to believe the law.
For this he came and won his trophies in secret,
And God was man, so that he might have us in the time to come.
But very many perish, who think they can please both,
Idols and God, though no one can please two.
There is one God in heaven, the God of heaven, earth and sea,
Whom Moses taught would hang on the tree for us.
Hence some senseless people go astray because he suffered such things,
Not paying enough attention to the hidden mystery of God.
Through the devil's envy death entered the world,
And God destroyed it secretly, born of a virgin.
At this birth the blind Jews lose their wits,
And, bloodstained from the crime they committed, they befool the foolish.
No one can offer any excuse hereafter,
Since the power to believe has now been given to us.
Not in vain did the Lord come down to earth from heaven,
But he came to make a people called by his name.
If anyone has not confessed him in this life,
He loses even the life he has lived, and cries out too late in punishment;
Or surely, while he hopes and waits to believe when he is grey,
He dies and is shut out from eternal life all the longer.
Therefore we ought now to turn our minds to him quickly,
Who promises to give us back life after death.
Besides this he adds that we shall be immortal
And shall enjoy seeing what the eye had never seen before.
These things will come when six thousand years are completed,
By which time I hope we ourselves will already be on the shore of the harbor.
Then man will rise, brought back in the sun's course,
And will rejoice in God, remembering what he was before;
He who heard the promises when he was frail in his former flesh,
Now incorrupt, recognizes what was promised before.
Marveling at the glory that has come to man, he speaks thus:
As I heard before, so I see each thing.
All who are raised from the underworld cry out together:
As we heard before, so, see, we behold!
All pain will leave the body, every sore will leave it,
Nor will there be any anxiety, only joy forever.
Whoever believes in three and perceives that one is present,
He will live everlasting, reborn into the eternal ages.
But some say: When do we suppose these things will come?
Hear in a few words after what events they will follow.
Many signs indeed will herald the end of so great a scourge,
But the beginning will be our seventh persecution.
See, already he knocks at the door and girds himself with a sword,
He who will soon cross the river as the Goths burst in.
King Apollyon will be with them, dreadful in name,
Who will scatter the persecution of the saints by force of arms.
He marches on Rome with many thousands of his race
And by God's decree takes captive those he has partly subdued.
Then many senators, made captive, will lament
And blaspheme the God of heaven, conquered by a barbarian.
Yet these pagans feed the Christians everywhere,
And seek them out rather as brothers, full of joy.
For the luxurious and those who worship empty idols
They persecute, and send the senate under the yoke.
These evils fall upon those who persecuted the beloved:
For five months they are slaughtered under this enemy.
Meanwhile, at that very time, Cyrus arises,
To terrify the enemy and set the senate free from there.
He returns from the underworld, who had been snatched from his throne
And long kept in reserve, recognizable in his former body.
We say that this is Nero of old,
Who earlier put Peter and Paul to death in the city.
He returns again at the very end of the age
From hidden places, he who was kept in reserve for this.
The senate itself marvels to see him;
When he appears, they will think him a god.
But before he comes, Elijah will prophesy
For a divided time, at the midpoint of the week.
When that span is complete, that abominable one follows,
Whom the Jews, together with the Romans, will then worship.
Though there will be another, whom they await from the east,
Yet they will rage in slaughtering us together with King Nero.
So when Elijah prophesies in the land of Judea
And marks the people with a sign in the name of Christ,
Since very many of them will not believe him,
In anger he begs the Most High that from then on it may not rain:
The sky will be shut from that time, nor will it be moist with dew,
And in his anger he turns the rivers too into blood.
The earth grows barren and no longer sweats with springs of water,
So that famine sets in; then there will also be plague in the world.
Because he does these things, the Jews, tormented indeed,
Concoct many false charges against him,
And first stir the senate to rise up in anger,
And say that Elijah acts as an enemy of the Romans.
Then the senate, at once stirred up by them,
Entreat Nero with prayers and wicked gifts:
Remove the enemies of the people from the world of men,
Through whom our gods too are trampled underfoot and not worshiped.
And he, filled with fury and moved by the senate's prayers,
Has the prophets seized from the east by the public post.
To satisfy the senators, or rather the Jews,
He slaughters these first, and then goes out against the churches.
At their martyrdom a tenth part of the city collapses,
And a full seven thousand people perish there.
But on the fourth day the Lord takes them up into the air,
Those whom, as they lay, their foes had forbidden to be buried;
And they are raised from the ground, made immortal out of death,
And their enemies look up and see them going through the air.
Not even so are they terrified, but grow more cruel within,
Cursing the people of Christ with utter hatred.
For the Most High hardened their wicked hearts,
As he had hardened Pharaoh's ears before.
So this harsh and wicked king, Nero, who had once been put to flight,
Orders the Christian people to be driven out of the city itself,
And takes to himself two Caesars as partners,
With whom to persecute this people with dreadful fury.
They send out edicts through all the judges everywhere,
To make this race of men be without the name of Christ.
They also command that incense be offered to images,
And, so that no one may hide, that all come forth wearing garlands.
In this ordeal, if a believer refuses to go,
It will be well with him; but if not, he becomes one of the crowd.
There will then be no day of peace, nor any offering to Christ,
But blood flows everywhere, which I cannot bring myself to describe;
For tears overcome me, my hand fails, my heart trembles,
Though it is fitting for martyrs to bear so many deaths;
Through sea, through lands, through islands and hiding places
They search long, and lead off the accursed as victims.
This Nero will then do for the whole space of three years,
And with half a year more he completes the appointed times.
For his crime a deadly vengeance will come,
So that the city and that people will be handed over together with him,
And the empire will be taken away, which was filled with wickedness,
And which for so long wore everyone down with harsh taxes.
In the downfall of this Nero there will arise in turn
A king from the east, with four nations from there,
And he summons to his side very many nations against the city
To bring him help, though he himself is very strong,
And he will fill the sea with many thousands of ships,
And whoever meets him will be slain by the sword;
First he takes Tyre and Sidon captive and subdues them,
and so the neighbouring nations grow faint with terror.
Here plague, here wars, here famine, here harsh tidings
are all mingled together, so that minds are thrown into confusion.
Meanwhile a trumpet suddenly blares from heaven,
(895) and its sound troubles hearts in every place.
Then a fiery chariot will be seen among the stars,
and a racing torch, to announce fire to the nations.
Then at last the whole river Euphrates is dried up,
so that a way may be prepared for the king and those nations.
Persians, Medes, Chaldeans and Babylonians will come together,
fierce and swift, who know no pity for anyone.
So when this man rises up and begins to advance from there,
Nero and the senate are thrown into confusion as soon as he is seen.
Those three Caesars will march out to resist him,
but he slaughters them and gives them to the birds for food.
Their armies have no choice but to worship the victor,
and returning with him to the City, their minds now changed,
they despoil the temples, and whatever is in the City
they plunder, and slaughter the men with enormous bloodshed;
at the very last they set fire to her and leave her stripped bare,
so that not even a trace of her is seen any more.
At her destruction the hearts of the powerful waste away,
and, stupefied, they cannot even tell what time they are living in.
She used to rejoice while the whole earth groaned;
yet a fitting retribution has scarcely come upon her.
She who boasted that she was eternal mourns for eternity,
and her tyrants too are then judged by the Most High.
As Rome smokes, the time stands ripe for the end,
and reward will come, apportioned according to what each place deserves.
From there, however, the victor marches into the land of Judea,
he whom the Jews themselves had watched conquer Rome.
He performs many signs so that they may believe in him,
since the wicked one has been sent to lead them astray;
yet the voice of the Most High, sounding from heaven, rebukes him.
This man from Persia declares that he is immortal.
For us Nero became the Antichrist; that other is the Antichrist for the Jews.
These two are always the prophets of the final end.
Nero is the ruin of the City, the other of the whole earth;
of him, however, I offer only a few things that I have read in secret writings.
Meanwhile, late though it is, even the Jews themselves come to dislike him [?],
and murmur among themselves that they have been deceived by fraud.
With one voice they cry out to heaven, weeping,
that the true God may come to their aid from on high.
Then God almighty, to bring all that I have told to its end,
will bring forth a people hidden for a long time.
They are Jews, shut in by a river beyond Persia,
whom God willed to remain there until the end.
Captivity brought them there to dwell;
of the twelve tribes, nine and a half live there.
There is no lying there, nor any hatred;
and so no son dies before his parents.
They do not lament or mourn the dead as we do,
since they await the resurrection to come.
They eat no living creature as part of their food,
but only vegetables, so that no blood is shed.
Full of righteousness, they live with bodies undefiled,
and impious fate exerts no power over them.
No fevers come upon them, no cruel chills,
since they obey everything in the pure law,
which we too shall follow when we live purely.
Only death and toil came to them; all else was powerless over them.
This people, then, now laid away beyond the river,
will return to the land of Judea when the river is dried up;
and God will come with them to fulfil his promises,
and all along the way they rejoice in God's presence.
Everything grows green before them, everything rejoices;
creation itself is glad to welcome the saints.
Everywhere springs rise up, ready to serve them,
wherever the people of the Most High march, in heavenly awe.
The clouds give them shade so that the sun does not trouble them,
and so that they do not grow weary, the very mountains lay themselves low;
for an angel of the Most High will be sent ahead of them
to give them peaceful guidance as they go.
They walk lightly on their way without toil,
and like lions they lay waste everything they pass through.
No nation will be able to resist them
if it makes war on them, since God himself is with them.
They conquer nations and bring down cities;
by God's permission they empty every settlement,
and grow rich with gold and silver from their plunder,
and so together they sing hymns of honour.
Soon they hasten to the holy city of their fathers,
and that terrible tyrant will be struck with terror
and flee to the kings of the North in great commotion,
and from there he snatches up a host, to stand and fight back as it were.
But when the rebels rush against the army of God,
they are struck to the ground by angels as battle is joined;
and the adulterer is seized, and his false prophet,
and they are cast alive into the lake, under fiery punishment.
Of their followers, the chief men, officers or envoys,
the wicked are reduced to being the slaves of the saints.
Meanwhile the saints enter the holy settlement,
to receive God's promises, rejoicing without end.
They entreat God that the dead may rise again,
as he long ago promised concerning the first resurrection.
Then God will begin to show his wrath against his enemies,
since the appointed day has come for the wicked.
When he begins to judge the world by fire,
the fire passes over the godly and falls on the ungodly.
Barely a few remain to tell of such deeds,
and those who are kept back to serve the righteous escape.
After the persecution of the saints and so many deaths,
the hateful, burning day is about to come.
Look, a hoarse trumpet sounds from heaven, echoing everywhere,
terrifying the whole world as it falls to ruin.
The sun flees without warning, and suddenly it looks like night,
and God cries out: “How long did you think I would bear with you?”
At his signal destruction rushes through the whole sky,
and with a crash of thunder the onslaught of fire descends.
Then bolt after bolt of lightning is hurled from the stars;
the fiery storm held back for so many years rages.
The deadly disaster roars, the earth is shaken and trembles,
and the whole human race cannot see where to turn.
The stars of heaven fall; the heavenly bodies are judged along with us;
the dwellers in heaven are troubled while the ruin of the world goes on.
Then there will be no help, and crying out will be in vain;
no ship will take anyone in, no hiding place either;
nor will those whom they once worshipped as great come to their aid.
Each man struggles for himself, but it will do him no good;
it will help only those who have been marked by Christ.
For them it will be as dew; for the rest, deadly punishment.
Some of the unbelievers are kept, only lightly scorched,
so that their race may lament once more at the very last.
Wherever people turn, the fiery force blazes;
the very air of the world, once so pleasant, is burned up.
How can I tell of all the crashes of the sky as it bears down with lightning,
when all the wrath stored up for so many years is poured out?
Here fire, here thunder, here whirlwinds, so many evils seethe,
and the sky is snatched away into shadow by the sudden force of death.
In some places the trembling earth loosens all its foundations;
in others thunderbolts burst apart strong ramparts,
and walls are scattered like dust into the air;
stones fly, and the roofs of houses are stripped off by the winds.
Homelands are laid waste, every city is levelled,
[?] … gives a kiss to the footprint [?].
So many crashes, so many roars, so much ruin —
who will be able to bear them, or escape such shipwreck?
What will a poor mother do then for her sweet little child?
Or if a father shows tender love to his son, what good will it do him?
Woe to those who have fled from the Lord, woe to the wicked who are without Christ,
among whom both those who rejoice and those who weep devoutly are judged!
All nature, moreover, will lament with bellowing
until at last the heavenly fury is spent and ceases.
Then for seven months the earth will be cleansed by fire,
and he who was lowly is seen coming from heaven.
With him will descend the angels of eternal glory;
the tombs will burst open, and the bodies of the righteous will rise,
and the clouds will snatch them up and carry them to meet Christ
in the air; the living saints receive the Lord.
He also raises up those others so that they may see his glory,
the one they nailed to the cross; but he will cast them back into the depths.
Woe to those wretched people! The Witness was put to death by them.
Which, for their punishments, foreseeing, by guile [?] …
We do not sing these things out of malice; we see that they are fixed.
While the righteous rejoice, those others are burned in hell;
David said of them: “Lord, repay them for their wickedness!”
And if they have not believed, they will go away into the shadow of death.
He could surely have prayed for good things for his people;
why did he wish instead: “Let them go down alive below”?
The rest of the saints who are alive at the coming of Christ,
